'''Reshef Tenne''' ({{Langx|he|רשף טנא}}; born September 2, 1944) is an Israeli physical and inorganic chemist and materials scientist, Professor Emeritus in the Faculty of Chemistry at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]]. Formerly head of the Department of Materials and Interfaces, he is a recipient of the Von Hippel Award, the [[EMET Prize]], and the Rothschild Prize, and a member of the Israel [[National Academy of Sciences]]. He is a world-renowned expert in layered materials. In 2026, he received the [[Israel Prize]] for Chemistry and Chemical Engineering Research.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Trabelsi-Hadad |first=Tamar |date=2026-02-01 |title=Israel Prize Laureate in Chemistry and Chemical Engineering Research - Prof. Reshef Tenne |url=https://www.ynetnews.com/article/p7q66pie6 |access-date=2026-03-09 |work=Ynetglobal |language=en}}</ref>

== Biography ==

=== Early life ===
Reshef Tenne was born in Kibbutz Usha, the son of Shoshana (née Hermelin)<ref>{{Cite web |title=דפי הנצחה - אושה- קהילנט |url=https://www.k-usha.org.il/http_new/viewpage.asp?pagesCatID=13495&MemorialPage=1&Personkey=84A070229ADDBFD5&siteName=usha |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=www.k-usha.org.il}}</ref> and Daniel "Danche" Tenne (originally Tannenbaum).<ref>{{Cite web |title=דפי הנצחה - אושה- קהילנט |url=https://www.k-usha.org.il/http_new/viewpage.asp?pagesCatID=13495&MemorialPage=1&Personkey=B78740E7C93F6691&siteName=usha |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=www.k-usha.org.il}}</ref> His parents immigrated from Poland and Belarus, settled initially in [[Magdiel]], and then moved to [[Usha, Israel|Usha]], where Reshef and his two siblings, Ruthie and Reuven, were born. Reshef was born in a tent because his parents had cleared their shack for new immigrants.<ref name=":0">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=whudhjw8FxY |title=ריאיון עם פרופ' רשף טנא חבר האקדמיה |date=2018-12-27 |last=The Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities |access-date=2025-08-30 |via=YouTube}}</ref> He was educated at Gush Zevulun School, where he studied under Haim Hadomi and Avraham Lifshitz, among others, but finished his studies without a matriculation certificate, as it was not customary in the kibbutz movement. He did a year of service in Kibbutz [[Gezer (kibbutz)|Gezer]] and in 1963 enlisted in military service in the [[35th Paratroopers Brigade (Israel)|Paratroopers Brigade]]. During his service, his father died prematurely,<ref>{{Cite web |title=⁨נפטר דניאל טנא ממייסדי אושא ⁩ {{!}} ⁨הבקר⁩ {{!}} 17 ספטמבר 1964 {{!}} אוסף העיתונות {{!}} הספרייה הלאומית |url=https://www.nli.org.il/he/newspapers/hbkr/1964/09/17/01/article/92 |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=www.nli.org.il |language=he}}</ref> and he then began to complete his matriculation certificate, finishing it after his discharge.<ref name=":0" />

=== Beginning of his academic career ===
Tenne began his undergraduate studies in chemistry at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem|Hebrew University]], completing them in 1969. He continued to pursue a master's degree in chemistry under the supervision of Prof. Gabriel Stein and PhD student (in later times Prof.) Yehuda Haas, working on the photochemical reduction of water to hydrogen using europium for solar energy production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=פוטוכימיה ופלואורסצנסיה של‏ (III)EU ‏בתמיסות מימיות |url=https://huji.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma990009867110203701&context=L&vid=972HUJI_INST:972HUJI_V1&lang=en&search_scope=MyInst_and_CI&adaptor=Local%20Search%20Engine&tab=Search_Options&query=any,contains,%D7%A8%D7%A9%D7%A3%20%D7%98%D7%A0%D7%90&offset=0 |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=huji.primo.exlibrisgroup.com |language=en}}</ref> From 1971 to 1976, he studied for a doctorate in [[theoretical chemistry]], under the joint supervision of Prof. [[Arieh Ben-Naim|Arieh Ben Naim]] and Prof. Shalom Baer. He completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Battelle Institute in Geneva under the supervision of Dr. Erich Bergmann and returned to Israel in 1979.<ref name=":0" />

=== As an independent researcher ===
Upon his return to Israel, Tenne joined Prof. Joost Manassen's research group, where he worked alongside Dr. Gary Hodes and Dr. [[David Cahen]] on photoelectrochemical cells.<ref name=":0" /> About two years later, he was appointed senior researcher. In 1983, he acquired the first [[electron microscope]] for materials research at the Weizmann Institute, which was shared by the faculties of chemistry and life sciences and formed the basis for what would become the Department of Chemical Research Support. In 1985, he was appointed Associate Professor, and in 1995, Full Professor. In 2014, he retired but continues to conduct active research to this day (2025). Tenne served as a visiting researcher at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology|Technion]], the [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] (Paris VI) in Paris, [[French National Centre for Scientific Research|CNRS]] Meudon, the [[University of Tokyo]], and the Helmholtz Institute for Renewable Energies (formerly [[Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin|Hahn-Meitner Institute]]) in Berlin. From 2000 to 2007, he served as head of the Department of Materials and Interfaces in the Faculty of Chemistry, and in 2003, he founded the Helen and Martin Kimmel Center for Nanoscale Science and was its first director until his retirement. He was the first recipient of the Drake Family Professorial chair in Nanotechnology (2004–2014). After his election as a member of the Israel National Academy of Sciences, he served for nearly a decade as head of the Committee for the Triennial Report on the State of Science in Israel, which is submitted to the [[Knesset]] (the Israeli Parliament).<ref>{{Cite web |title=דוח מצב המדע בישראל של האקדמיה הלאומית הישראלית למדעים הוגש לנשיא המדינה |url=https://www.academy.ac.il/News/NewsItem.aspx?nodeId=658&id=2489 |website=Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities}}</ref>

== Research ==
Since the early 1980s, Tenne has been engaged in research on layered materials, and he is probably the longest-active researcher in the world working on this topic. These materials have an intra-layer structure based on strong covalent bonds, and an inter-layer structure based on weak [[van der Waals force]]s. These materials possess highly anisotropic physio-chemical properties that are fundamentally different from materials with three-dimensional symmetry, such as [[gallium arsenide]]. Early in his independent research career, he studied tungsten diselenide, and after a few years, he moved on to prepare thin films of [[molybdenum disulfide]] and [[tungsten disulfide]], with the aim of using them to fabricate photovoltaic cells. In 1992, he discovered that in analogy to carbon fullerenes and nanotubes, nanoparticles of compounds with layered structure, like {{chem2|WS2}} and {{chem2|MoS2}} form hollow spherical [[nanoparticle]]s, which he nicknamed [[Transition metal fullerene complex|fullerene-like]] (IF) and [[nanotube]]s (INT), respectively. Initially he collaborated with the electron microscopy expert Dr. Lev Margulis and later on with Dr. Ronit Popovitz-Biro.<ref name=":0" /> Since 2010, he has been working on nanotubes from misfit layered compounds (MLC), which are made of at least three elements.<ref name=":0" />

Throughout his years as a researcher, Tenne authored some 500 articles and supervised about 70 research students, including Prof. Gitti Frey,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Frey, Gitti L. |url=https://weizmann.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma990001467010203596&context=L&vid=972WIS_INST:972WIS_V1&lang=en&search_scope=All_Institution_and_CentralIndex&adaptor=Local%20Search%20Engine&tab=Everything&query=any,contains,%D7%92%D7%99%D7%98%D7%99%20%D7%A4%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%99%20%D7%A8%D7%A9%D7%A3%20%D7%98%D7%A0%D7%90&offset=0&pcAvailability=true |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=weizmann.primo.exlibrisgroup.com |language=en}}</ref> currently the Dean of the Faculty of Materials Engineering in the Technion and Prof. Maya Bar-Sadan,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bar-Sadan, Maya |url=https://weizmann.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma990001207580203596&context=L&vid=972WIS_INST:972WIS_V1&lang=en&search_scope=All_Institution_and_CentralIndex&adaptor=Local%20Search%20Engine&tab=Everything&query=any,contains,%D7%9E%D7%90%D7%99%D7%94%20%D7%91%D7%A8%20%D7%A1%D7%93%D7%9F&offset=0&pcAvailability=true |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=weizmann.primo.exlibrisgroup.com |language=en}}</ref> the head of the Department of Chemistry in [[Ben-Gurion University of the Negev]]. Many researchers who worked under his supervision have joined the industry.

=== Discovery of Inorganic Nanotubes and Fullerene-like Inorganic Nanoparticles ===
[[Linus Pauling]] proposed in 1930 that layered (two-dimensional) materials with an asymmetric structure along the 'a' axis, such as chrysotile and halloysite, would spontaneously curl to form cylindrical or helical structures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pauling |first=Linus |date=1930 |title=The Structure of the Micas and Related Minerals |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.16.2.123 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=123–129 |doi=10.1073/pnas.16.2.123 |pmc=1075954 |pmid=16587535}}</ref> This proposal was confirmed in 1950 by Bates et al. when chrysotile nanotubes were first observed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bates |first=Thomas F. |last2=Sand |first2=Leonard B. |last3=Mink |first3=John F. |date=1950-05-12 |title=Tubular Crystals of Chrysotile Asbestos |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.111.2889.512 |journal=Science |volume=111 |issue=2889 |pages=512–513 |doi=10.1126/science.111.2889.512|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Following the discovery of carbon fullerenes in 1985, Kroto proposed that graphite nanoparticles suffer from internal instability due to dangling bonds at the edge atoms, causing them to fold and close into fullerenes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kroto |first=H. W. |date=1987 |title=The stability of the fullerenes Cn, with n = 24, 28, 32, 36, 50, 60 and 70 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/329529a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=329 |issue=6139 |pages=529–531 |doi=10.1038/329529a0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This idea was later extended to carbon nanotubes by Iijima (1991),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iijima |first=Sumio |last2=Ichihashi |first2=Toshinari |date=1993 |title=Single-shell carbon nanotubes of 1-nm diameter |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/363603a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=363 |issue=6430 |pages=603–605 |doi=10.1038/363603a0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which led Tenne to propose (1992) that nanoparticles of inorganic layered compounds, such as tungsten disulfide and molybdenum disulfide, also suffer from similar instability and form hollow closed structures – i.e., inorganic nanotubes (INT) and inorganic fullerene-like nanoparticles (IF).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tenne |first=R. |last2=Margulis |first2=L. |last3=Genut |first3=M. |last4=Hodes |first4=G. |date=1992 |title=Polyhedral and cylindrical structures of tungsten disulphide |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/360444a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=360 |issue=6403 |pages=444–446 |doi=10.1038/360444a0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Margulis |first=L. |last2=Salitra |first2=G. |last3=Tenne |first3=R. |last4=Talianker |first4=M. |date=1993 |title=Nested fullerene-like structures |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/365113b0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=365 |issue=6442 |pages=113–114 |doi=10.1038/365113b0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Tenne 1995 965–995">{{Cite journal |last=Tenne |first=Reshef |date=1995 |title=Doped and heteroatom-containing fullerene-like structures and nanotubes |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adma.19950071203 |journal=Advanced Materials |language=de |volume=7 |issue=12 |pages=965–995 |doi=10.1002/adma.19950071203 |issn=1521-4095|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Subsequently, nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles of many other two-dimensional materials were synthesized and studied, including {{chem2|BN}}, {{chem2|NiCl2}}, {{chem2|Cs2O}}, {{chem2|Tl2O}}, {{chem2|NiClOH}}, {{chem2|TaS2}}, {{chem2|H2Ti3O7}}, {{chem2|V2O5}}, and more. Additional types of nanotubes from two-dimensional materials were investigated using computer simulations.

Tenne extended this concept in recent years and synthesized many kinds of nanotubes from the non-stoichiometric misfit layered compounds with a structure of the form (MX)<sub>1+γ</sub>(TX<sub>2</sub>)<sub>m</sub>, where M is an element like bismuth, antimony, tin, lead, or another rare element; T can be [[niobium]], tantalum, titanium, vanadium, or chromium; X is sulfur or selenium; and γ ranges from 0.08 to 0.28. In these cases, both the Pauling mechanism (asymmetry along the 'a' axis) and the dangling bond edge-closure mechanism (Kroto-Iijima-Tenne mechanism) act conjointly, leading to a high yield of nanotubes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Panchakarla |first=Leela S. |last2=Radovsky |first2=Gal |last3=Houben |first3=Lothar |last4=Popovitz-Biro |first4=Ronit |last5=Dunin-Borkowski |first5=Rafal E. |last6=Tenne |first6=Reshef |date=2014-11-06 |title=Nanotubes from Misfit Layered Compounds: A New Family of Materials with Low Dimensionality |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters |volume=5 |issue=21 |pages=3724–3736 |doi=10.1021/jz5016845}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sreedhara |first=M. B. |last2=Hettler |first2=Simon |last3=Kaplan-Ashiri |first3=Ifat |last4=Rechav |first4=Katya |last5=Feldman |first5=Yishay |last6=Enyashin |first6=Andrey |last7=Houben |first7=Lothar |last8=Arenal |first8=R. |last9=Tenne |first9=Reshef |date=2021-08-31 |title=Asymmetric misfit nanotubes: Chemical affinity outwits the entropy at high-temperature solid-state reactions |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.2109945118 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=118 |issue=35 |article-number=e2109945118 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2109945118 |pmc=8536368 |pmid=34446565}}</ref> It can be stated that inorganic nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles are metastable nanoscale manifestations of layered compounds, and can be prepared from a wide range of elements and compounds – from insulators to semiconductors, metals, and superconductors. These nanoparticles can be distinguished from the original bulk material using any available physio-chemical method.

=== Strategies for Synthesizing Nanotubes and Fullerene-like Nanoparticles ===
Tenne and his team developed new chemical strategies for synthesizing various types of nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles from layered compounds, including metal dichalcogenides, halides, and oxides.

For this purpose, they used a variety of high-temperature techniques, such as chemical vapor transport, [[chemical vapor deposition]], [[laser ablation]], focused solar radiation, electron beam, microwave, and mechanical shock. In particular, in-depth research into the conversion of metal oxides to sulfides (or selenides) at high temperatures revealed a "surface inwards" and more recently also the "receding oxide core" mechanisms for nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Feldman |first=Y. |last2=Frey |first2=G. L. |last3=Homyonfer |first3=M. |last4=Lyakhovitskaya |first4=V. |last5=Margulis |first5=L. |last6=Cohen |first6=H. |last7=Hodes |first7=G. |last8=Hutchison |first8=J. L. |last9=Tenne |first9=R. |date=1996-01-01 |title=Bulk Synthesis of Inorganic Fullerene-like MS2 (M = Mo, W) from the Respective Trioxides and the Reaction Mechanism |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=118 |issue=23 |pages=5362–5367 |doi=10.1021/ja9602408 |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zak |first=A. |last2=Feldman |first2=Y. |last3=Alperovich |first3=V. |last4=Rosentsveig |first4=R. |last5=Tenne |first5=R. |date=2000-11-01 |title=Growth Mechanism of MoS2 Fullerene-like Nanoparticles by Gas-Phase Synthesis |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=122 |issue=45 |pages=11108–11116 |doi=10.1021/ja002181a |issn=0002-7863}}</ref> Subsequently, a large-scale process for producing pure phases of IF nanoparticles and nanotubes of {{chem2|WS<sub>2</sub>}} was developed in his laboratory. These studies paved the way for the commercialization of the particles for a variety of applications.

New strategies in high-temperature materials chemistry were developed for controlled doping of tungsten disulfide and molybdenum disulfide nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles with trace amounts of rhenium and niobium.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deepak |first=Francis Leonard |last2=Cohen |first2=Hagai |last3=Cohen |first3=Sidney |last4=Feldman |first4=Yishay |last5=Popovitz-Biro |first5=Ronit |last6=Azulay |first6=Doron |last7=Millo |first7=Oded |last8=Tenne |first8=Reshef |date=2007-10-01 |title=Fullerene-Like (IF) NbxMo1-xS2 Nanoparticles |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=129 |issue=41 |pages=12549–12562 |doi=10.1021/ja074081b |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yadgarov |first=Lena |last2=Rosentsveig |first2=Rita |last3=Leitus |first3=Gregory |last4=Albu-Yaron |first4=Ana |last5=Moshkovich |first5=Alexey |last6=Perfilyev |first6=Vladislav |last7=Vasic |first7=Relja |last8=Frenkel |first8=Anatoly I. |last9=Enyashin |first9=Andrey N. |last10=Seifert |first10=Gotthard |last11=Rapoport |first11=Lev |last12=Tenne |first12=Reshef |date=2012 |title=Controlled Doping of MS2 (M=W, Mo) Nanotubes and Fullerene-like Nanoparticles |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/anie.201105324 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |volume=51 |issue=5 |pages=1148–1151 |doi=10.1002/anie.201105324 |issn=1521-3773|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rosentsveig |first=Rita |last2=Yadgarov |first2=Lena |last3=(Isai) Feldman |first3=Yishay |last4=Shilstein |first4=Sana |last5=Popovitz-Biro |first5=Ronit |last6=Visic |first6=Bojana |last7=Sedova |first7=Anastasiya |last8=Cohen |first8=Sidney R. |last9=Li |first9=Yuanyuan |last10=Frenkel |first10=Anatoly I. imparted negative or positive [[surface charge]] density to the particles, respectively, and facilitated their dispersion in various liquids. In addition, hints of a phase transition from a stable (2H) semiconducting state to a metastable (1T) conducting state were found in structures doped with rhenium. The doped particles showed improved catalytic properties for hydrogen generation and improved tribological properties, likely due to self-repulsion between the surface-charged doped nanoparticles, preventing their agglomeration and precipitation.

Already at an early stage of his research, Tenne raised the possibility of hollow molybdenum disulfide nano-octahedra as the smallest fullerene-like nanostructure.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Tenne 1995 965–995"/> These particles were later produced by laser ablation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Parilla |first=P. A. |last2=Dillon |first2=A. C. |last3=Jones |first3=K. M. |last4=Riker |first4=G. |last5=Schulz |first5=D. L. |last6=Ginley |first6=D. S. |last7=Heben |first7=M. These structures are expected to also appear in many other layered compounds, and to provide a platform for new catalytic mechanisms.

Tenne predicted,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rapoport |first=L. |last2=Bilik |first2=Yu |last3=Feldman |first3=Y. |last4=Homyonfer |first4=M. |last5=Cohen |first5=S. R. |last6=Tenne |first6=R. |date=1997 |title=Hollow nanoparticles of WS2 as potential solid-state lubricants |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/42910 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=387 |issue=6635 |pages=791–793 |doi=10.1038/42910 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and later proved,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tevet |first=Ofer |last2=Von-Huth |first2=Palle |last3=Popovitz-Biro |first3=Ronit |last4=Rosentsveig |first4=Rita |last5=Wagner |first5=H. Daniel |last6=Tenne |first6=Reshef |date=2011-12-13 |title=Friction mechanism of individual multilayered nanoparticles |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1106553108 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=108 |issue=50 |pages=19901–19906 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1106553108 |pmc=3250150 |pmid=22084073}}</ref> that fullerene-like nanoparticles of tungsten disulfide and molybdenum disulfide behave like spherical bearings at the nanometer level, providing exceptional solid lubrication capabilities. This work revealed a new lubrication mechanism based on the rolling of nanoparticles, characterized by a very low coefficient of friction. Furthermore, the work opened a window to a new lubrication technology, which is used for various tribological applications. Several companies are already producing and marketing these products, and medical technologies based on this corpus of work have been proposed and are under development.

=== Characterization of Tungsten Disulfide Nanotubes and Nanoparticles ===
The unique mechanical properties of tungsten disulfide nanotubes and fullerene-like nanoparticles were investigated in Tenne's laboratory using a variety of methods. They were found to withstand pressure waves of up to 21 gigapascals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zhu |first=Y. Q. |last2=Sekine |first2=T. |last3=Li |first3=Y. H. |last4=Wang |first4=W. X. |last5=Fay |first5=M. W. |last6=Edwards |first6=H. |last7=Brown |first7=P. D. |last8=Fleischer |first8=N. |last9=Tenne |first9=R. |date=2005 |title=WS2 and MoS2 Inorganic Fullerenes—Super Shock Absorbers at Very High Pressures |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adma.200401962 |journal=Advanced Materials |volume=17 |issue=12 |pages=1500–1503 |doi=10.1002/adma.200401962 |issn=1521-4095|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Experiments of stretching, bending, and twisting on individual nanotubes showed that they possess a strength of up to 20 gigapascals – four times that of Kevlar fibers – and can withstand strains of over 10% without breaking.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kaplan-Ashiri |first=Ifat |last2=Cohen |first2=Sidney R. |last3=Gartsman |first3=Konstantin |last4=Ivanovskaya |first4=Viktoria |last5=Heine |first5=Thomas |last6=Seifert |first6=Gotthard |last7=Wiesel |first7=Inna |last8=Wagner |first8=H. Daniel |last9=Tenne |first9=Reshef |date=2006-01-17 |title=On the mechanical behavior of WS2 nanotubes under axial tension and compression |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.0505640103 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=103 |issue=3 |pages=523–528 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0505640103 |pmc=1334634 |pmid=16407141}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sadan |first=Maya Bar |last2=Houben |first2=Lothar |last3=Enyashin |first3=Andrey N. |last4=Seifert |first4=Gotthard |last5=Tenne |first5=Reshef |date=2008-10-14 |title=Atom by atom: HRTEM insights into inorganic nanotubes and fullerene-like structures |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.0805407105 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=105 |issue=41 |pages=15643–15648 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0805407105 |pmc=2572970 |pmid=18838681}}</ref> These properties make them suitable for reinforcing polymer nanocomposites. Such nanocomposites, containing up to 1% by weight of tungsten disulfide nanotubes or IF nanoparticles, showed improved mechanical, thermal, and tribological properties. In particular, the mechanical properties of biocompatible polymers such as PLLA, PVA, and PPF, used in medical technologies, food packaging, and tissue engineering, were improved significantly after the addition of small amounts of tungsten disulfide nanotubes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ramachandran |first=Karthik |last2=Shao |first2=Zixuan |last3=Di Luccio |first3=Tiziana |last4=Shen |first4=Bo |last5=Bello |first5=Edgar E. == Personal life ==
Until her death, Tenne was married to Leah (née Yonas), the founder of adult education frameworks in the city of Rehovot. They had a daughter, Dana, and sons Tal and Ron (currently a faculty member at the Technion).<ref>{{Cite web |title=רון טנא |url=https://chemistry.technion.ac.il/team/%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%9F-%D7%98%D7%A0%D7%90/ |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=הפקולטה לכימיה בטכניון |language=he-IL}}</ref> In memory of Leah Tenne, the Israel Chemical Society annually awards the "Tenne Family Prize in Nanoscience".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Tenne Family Prize for Nano Scale Sciences |url=https://www.chemistry.org.il/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/The-Tenne-Family-Prize.pdf}}</ref> After Leah's death, Tenne remarried Prof. Ella Zak (née Schreiber),<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-06-30 |title=צינוריות השֶׁמֶשׁ - מסע הקסם המדעי - חדשות מדע, תגליות ומידע לציבור |url=https://heb.wis-wander.weizmann.ac.il/chemistry/n-10234 |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=מסע הקסם המדעי - חדשות מדע, תגליות ומידע לציבור מבית מכון ויצמן למדע |language=he}}</ref> a faculty member and Dean of the Faculty of Sciences at Holon Institute of Technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=אלה זאק |url=https://www.hit.ac.il/staff/96739-alla-zak/ |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=מכון טכנולוגי חולון – HIT |language=he-IL}}</ref> In 2024, Zak and Tenne founded the Zak-Tenne Prize for Materials Science, awarded by the Israel Vacuum Society.<ref>{{Cite web |title=IVS-IPSTA 2024 - 41TH ANNUAL |url=https://www.ivs.org.il/ivs-ipsta-2024-41th-annual |access-date=2025-08-30 |website=IVS |language=en}}</ref> Tenne resides in Rehovot.

* Member of the Israel National Academy of Sciences (2011)

* Member of Academia Europaea (2012)

* Honorary Professor at Taiwan Technological University, Taipei (2015)

* IUVSTA Technology Award, Malmö (2019)
* EMET Prize (2020)

* [[Israel Prize]] for Chemistry and Chemical Engineering Research (2026)
